findings.title: asyncio.gather cancellation-then-first-exception pattern duplicated at several call sites; only the cancellation check was extracted, not the whole idiom
findings.problem: The mined theme (8 fix commits: 484, 512, 516, 647, 191/192, 519, 1151) shows CancelledError-swallowing across gather sites was a recurring bug class. propagate_cancellations (utils/async_utils.py:37) now correctly centralizes Pass-1 (re-raise structured cancellation before any per-item logging), but Pass-2 ('log every Exception, then raise/accumulate the first one') is still copy-pasted by hand at every call site with slightly different wording and behaviour (get_entity's two branches raise the first exception outright; rebuild_entity_summaries instead accumulates a per-entity error status and keeps going). Each new gather call site is a fresh chance to forget to call propagate_cancellations at all, or to get the exception-vs-continue policy wrong for that call site.
findings.proposal: Extend fused_memory.utils.async_utils with two named helpers built on propagate_cancellations: gather_or_raise(coros) (Pass1 + raise-first, for get_entity-style call sites that must fail the whole read on any error) and gather_collect(coros) (Pass1 + per-item Exception/success tuple, for rebuild_entity_summaries-style call sites that tolerate partial failure). Migrate all current call sites onto these, so the cancellation-safety contract is enforced by one tested function rather than re-derived at each new gather() site.

findings.title: The CancelledError re-raise convention used by most MCP tool handlers in tools.py is unenforced and already regressed in 4 task-routing handlers
findings.problem: 42 of the ~47 exception-catching @mcp.tool() functions in this file follow the convention 'except (asyncio.CancelledError, KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit): raise' immediately before a broader 'except Exception as e:' handler that converts errors into error-dict responses -- the same pattern the mined CancelledError fix theme addressed elsewhere (tasks 484/512/516/647/191/192/519). But the convention exists only as a repeated hand-written idiom with no shared decorator or lint rule enforcing it: submit_task, resolve_ticket, list_tickets, and cancel_ticket (task/ticket-routing tools in the same file) catch bare except Exception with no cancellation guard, so a cancellation delivered while these coroutines await task_interceptor.* gets silently converted into a normal error-dict response instead of propagating.
findings.proposal: Introduce an mcp_tool_errors(operation=...) decorator in tools.py that wraps the handler body, re-raises (CancelledError, KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit), and converts any other Exception to the standard error dict with logging -- then apply it uniformly to all @mcp.tool() functions, removing the 42 hand-copies and closing the 4 gaps so the invariant is structural rather than a convention that can silently regress per-function.

findings.title: Duplicated canonical stage->recon_pool constant map creates a drift-prone cross-module contract (mitigated but not removed)

clusters.hotspot: escalation subsystem: escalation/src/escalation/server.py (MCP tool surface + resolve_issue action/level gating), escalation/src/escalation/queue.py (filesystem-backed record store, locking, archive), and their consumer in orchestrator/src/orchestrator/harness.py (~9k lines) which owns the ONLY implementation of what each resolve_issue action actually does to a task/workflow.
clusters.architecture_notes: escalation/server.py is a thin, well-documented MCP tool layer: escalate_info/escalate_blocker (agent submit side, with a severity→level=2 "born-at-L2" stamp and a terminal-task auto-resolve chokepoint), resolve_issue (handler-side, a 5-value RESOLVE_ACTIONS enum: resume/restart/park/abandon/close_only), promote_to_l2 (watcher-only by convention), and merge/scheduler/warm-worktree control tools. queue.py is a filesystem store (esc-*.json + dated archive/ subdirs) with a real cross-process flock (escalation_id_lock, keyed on a stable sidecar file to defeat tmp+rename inode churn) and careful idempotent resolve()/park() semantics plus L2→member cascade. The critical split: resolve_issue only validates the action string and (optionally, via an HTTP-header capability gate) the caller's permitted levels; it stamps `resolution_action` on the record and calls queue.resolve()/park(), which only flip status pending→resolved/dismissed. What each action actually DOES to the task/workflow (re-pend, hard restart to pending, teardown to blocked, cancel) is decided entirely downstream, in orchestrator/harness.py's `_on_escalation_resolved` → `_resolve_escalation_action` → `_ACTION_TARGETS` dict / `_cascade_unblock_member` / `_action_teardown_and_set_status` — a second, independently-evolving interpretation of the same enum, guarded by ad hoc preconditions (level>=1, is_l2_cascade, task not in `_escalation_events`, status=='blocked') that silently no-op (DEBUG/INFO log, no error) when unmet rather than rejecting the caller. A dedicated design doc (plans/escalation-repend-state-machine-prd.md, D1-D11) already tried to make this coherent in 2026-06, but new task-specific branches (e.g. task 1883's infra_hold "resume-at-verify") have since been bolted onto `_cascade_unblock_member` without updating that design or the action-semantics table in resolve_issue's docstring, reintroducing exactly the ambiguity the PRD set out to remove. Capability control (which caller may act on which level) is an HTTP-header opt-in (`X-Escalation-Levels`) that is a no-op unless the specific client sends it — only the orchestrator's own auto-watcher does, via a hardcoded `_WATCHER_ESCALATION_HEADERS` dict in harness.py — so the enforcement that stopped the historical L1→L2 overstep is a self-imposed leash on one well-behaved client, not a server-side authorization boundary.
clusters.cross_system_notes: The `infra_hold` in-progress overload (finding 4) was driven by a limitation in the orchestrator's merge/dispatch subsystem, not by anything intrinsic to escalation: task 1883's commit messages cite "the 3465 starvation root cause" — the scheduler's footprint-locked dispatch would force a verify-complete branch to re-win its whole implement footprint if flipped to 'pending'. Rather than fixing dispatch to special-case "resume at verify, not at implement," the fix was made inside the escalation-resolution callback (_cascade_unblock_member), teaching it a second, non-obvious meaning for writing 'in-progress' that only escalation-adjacent code (and the stranded-recovery sweep, which had to grow a matching infra_hold guard) knows about. This is a defect in the dispatch/footprint-lock subsystem being patched around from the escalation-consumer side. Separately, the terminal-task auto-resolve chokepoint (`task_status_lookup`) makes escalation maintain its own belief about whether a task is 'done'/'cancelled', sourced from fused-memory via an injected callback — a second, parallel read of state whose source of truth is fused-memory's task table; no schema/contract pins what statuses that callback may return, so a new terminal-ish status introduced in fused-memory (e.g. a future 'merge-deferred' terminal variant) would silently fail to trip the chokepoint here.

findings.title: resolve_issue action semantics live in two files with no shared state-machine table, and preconditions fail silently
findings.problem: RESOLVE_ACTIONS (server.py:130, resolve_issue at 506-629) is validated as a bare string enum with no notion of which record states (level, category, whether a live workflow owns the task, whether the task is 'blocked' vs something else) each action is legal for. queue.resolve()/park() only check status=='pending' (queue.py:453-501, 535-547) — level, category, and current task status are invisible to them. The actual per-action effect on the task/workflow is reconstructed independently in harness.py's _on_escalation_resolved (7958-8085) and _cascade_unblock_member (8428-8511): 'resume' only flips blocked→pending if escalation.level>=1 AND (is_l2_cascade OR task_id not already tracked by a live workflow) AND the task's CURRENT status is literally 'blocked' — any other current status causes a DEBUG-level silent no-op with no error surfaced to the caller of resolve_issue. This is the exact shape of the documented stranded_blocked resume bug (operator memory: 'resume on stranded_blocked leaves task in-progress, not pending' / feedback_stranded_blocked_resume_leaves_in_progress.md, esc-2073-15).
findings.proposal: Introduce one authoritative transition table — e.g. escalation/src/escalation/state_machine.py exporting LEGAL_TRANSITIONS: dict[(action, level, category), TaskEffect] — imported by BOTH resolve_issue (to reject illegal action/state combos with a loud {'error':...,'code':'illegal_transition'} instead of silently mutating the record) and by harness.py's callback (to compute the task effect, replacing the ad hoc if/elif chain). Any precondition failure (task not in the expected pre-state) should raise/return a typed rejection surfaced to the resolver, not a DEBUG log the human never sees. This directly targets the recurring class the escalation-repend-state-machine-prd.md (D1-D11) tried to solve but which regressed once task 1883 added a new branch outside that design.
findings.bug_history_link: feedback_stranded_blocked_resume_leaves_in_progress.md (esc-2073-15, 2026-07-04); plans/escalation-repend-state-machine-prd.md (D1-D11, authored 2026-06-04) documents the same defect class this was meant to close

findings.title: Level-based capability gate (level_forbidden) is an HTTP-header opt-in, not a server-enforced authorization boundary
findings.problem: resolve_issue's level_forbidden check (server.py:565-592) only fires when the caller's transport happens to set the X-Escalation-Levels header; the function's own docstring/comments admit get_http_headers() returns {} for in-process tool.fn() calls and stdio transport, so the gate is a no-op for those callers ('default-open is preserved byte-for-byte'). The only caller that ever sends the header is the orchestrator's own auto-watcher, via the hardcoded _WATCHER_ESCALATION_HEADERS = {'X-Escalation-Levels': '0,1'} dict in harness.py:241-255. Any other MCP client (a differently-configured watcher, a buggy script, an interactive session that reuses agent_role='escalation-watcher-auto') can call resolve_issue(action='close_only'|'abandon', ...) on an L2 record with zero restriction, because the restriction is self-declared by the caller rather than derived from caller identity server-side.
findings.proposal: Move the level-gate from 'does the caller declare a restriction' to 'does the caller prove a capability': mint a signed/opaque capability token per connection type at MCP-session-establishment time (or at minimum require the identity header — already present as X-Escalation-Identity — to resolve to a role→allowed-levels mapping maintained server-side, e.g. a small ROLE_LEVEL_ALLOWLIST in server.py) so omitting the levels header defaults to the caller's role-derived ceiling rather than 'no restriction'. This closes the same hole that produced the L1→L2 overstep incident, but for the general case rather than just the one watcher client that was patched.
findings.bug_history_link: project_escalation_watcher_L2_is_orchestrator_autowatcher_2026_07_03.md — PRD 18d2a490e9 (df 2041-2044) added level_forbidden specifically for the auto-watcher's own header; this finding shows the same gap remains open for any other caller

findings.title: promote_to_l2 has no capability/role check on its create side
findings.problem: promote_to_l2 (server.py:682-807) explicitly bypasses the terminal-task chokepoint and the severity→level dedupe gate, minting a level=2 human-facing record directly via queue.submit()/add_members_to_l2(). Its docstring says 'this tool is for the auto-watcher' but agent_role is an unchecked free-form string parameter — nothing server-side restricts which callers may invoke it. Given the entire point of the L0→L1→L2 ladder is to gate access to the scarce human-attention channel, the RESOLVE side now has (a leaky, see finding 2) level check, but the CREATE side that mints new L2s has none at all.
findings.proposal: Reuse the same role→allowed-levels mapping proposed in finding 2 to gate promote_to_l2 symmetrically with resolve_issue: require the caller's declared/derived identity to be in an allowlist (e.g. {'escalation-watcher-auto', 'operator'}) before minting level=2, returning {'error':..., 'code':'level_forbidden'} otherwise. This is the missing half of the L1→L2 overstep fix — closing the write path, not just the resolve path.
findings.bug_history_link: companion gap to project_escalation_watcher_L2_is_orchestrator_autowatcher_2026_07_03.md; no direct incident yet observed — speculative but structurally identical to the resolved incident

findings.title: 'in-progress' status is overloaded with a second, ad hoc meaning (infra_hold) that must be tracked identically in two separate reconciliation call sites
findings.problem: _cascade_unblock_member (harness.py:8456-8490, task 1883 step-16) writes status='in-progress' for a stranded_blocked task carrying metadata.infra_hold, meaning something categorically different from the normal 'a live coroutine currently owns this task' meaning of in-progress — there is no live claimant started by this write. The ONLY thing that keeps this row from being permanently invisible to recovery is that _revert_in_progress_if_no_live_claimant (harness.py:3399-3454, also task 1883 step-14) independently re-checks the same metadata.infra_hold flag and skips the row while it's set. The invariant 'in-progress rows without infra_hold are eventually reconciled by plan.lock liveness; rows with infra_hold are deliberately exempt' is enforced by two hand-written flag checks in two different functions with no shared type or single-source-of-truth — a future caller that sets metadata.infra_hold without knowing about _revert_in_progress_if_no_live_claimant's guard (or vice versa) silently produces a permanently-orphaned in-progress task.
findings.proposal: Replace the metadata.infra_hold boolean with an explicit sub-status on TaskStatus (e.g. a real 'in-progress-hold-infra' state, or a typed `InProgressReason` enum stored once and read by both call sites via a single accessor function `is_infra_held(task) -> bool` in one module) so the exemption is expressed once and any new consumer of 'in-progress' is forced to go through it rather than re-deriving the flag check.
findings.bug_history_link: git log -S infra_hold: fccdbfd0a8 / d775e4e916 (task 1883, itself a workaround for the '3465 starvation' dispatch-footprint-lock defect); speculative that this has caused a second incident beyond esc-2073-15, but the structural gap is confirmed in code

findings.title: Escalation ID uniqueness is reconstructed by re-scanning two directory tiers plus a per-instance cache, rather than a single authoritative counter
findings.problem: make_id() (queue.py:1001-1039) derives the next sequence number by globbing the queue root fresh every call, combined with a per-task_id _archive_max_seq_cache that is explicitly documented as 'correct only for the single-writer model... a concurrent process archiving an escalation for a task_id whose entry is already seeded in this instance's cache will not reflect that higher seq'. get_by_task (queue.py:309-390) similarly reconstructs correctness via a manual cross-tier pre-scan + seen-set dedup rather than a single lookup. This is the area with the densest fix history in the mined themes (4x get_by_task dedup-before-filter fixes across duplicate tasks 999/1000/1001/1002; 6x archive/ID-collision hardening commits including 28feb9cd1e, baa7f96f0a/task 1879, 9cf4dd3b42/task 1324, 4c407593ff) — each round patched a specific manifestation (TOCTOU race, filter ordering, cache staleness) without removing the underlying re-derive-from-directory-scan design.
findings.proposal: Replace directory-scan-derived sequencing with a single durable counter file per task_id (fsync'd increment under the existing escalation_id_lock sidecar mechanism) as the sole source of the next sequence number, eliminating both the archive-scan cache-staleness class and the get_by_task cross-tier dedup class in one move — the lock primitive to do this safely already exists and is well-tested (escalation_id_lock, queue.py:24-69).
findings.bug_history_link: tasks 999/1000 (duplicate), 1001/1002 (duplicate follow-up), 1879 (baa7f96f0a), 1324 (9cf4dd3b42), 28feb9cd1e, 4c407593ff — 6+ discrete fix commits against the same design

findings.title: datetime.UTC vs timezone.utc flip-flopped 6x on a false 'Python <3.11 compat' premise never checked against pyproject
findings.problem: Six alternating commits (46d8aaec0b → ad76ac658f → 3545e5edfa → 50321469bd → 3e73e109ab) toggled server.py between datetime.UTC and timezone.utc, twice justified by 'Python <3.11 compat'. escalation/pyproject.toml pins requires-python = '>=3.11,<4' and selects ruff rule 'UP' (which includes UP017, the rule that mandates datetime.UTC once py311 is the floor) — so the compat rationale was factually false both times it was asserted, and nothing in the fix workflow checked the stated premise (requires-python) before committing a revert.
findings.proposal: No code fix needed beyond settling on datetime.UTC (already the current state); the systemic fix is procedural: fix-agents touching lint/typing churn should be required to grep the target package's requires-python / ruff target-version before asserting a version-compat rationale in a commit message, or CI should simply trust ruff's own UP017 finding as authoritative (it already knows the configured target-version) rather than allowing a manual override commit to fight the linter. Low-value to build tooling for a 6-commit churn, but worth a one-line convention note (e.g. in escalation's CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md or the verify skill) telling fix-agents to trust `ruff check` over ad hoc compat claims.
findings.bug_history_link: 46d8aaec0b, ad76ac658f, 3545e5edfa, 50321469bd, 3e73e109ab — mined theme '[6x] Timezone/UP017 datetime.UTC alias flip-flopping'

clusters.hotspot: dashboard/src/dashboard/data/ (merge_queue.py, orchestrator.py, costs.py, burndown.py) reading orchestrator-internal state (runs.db events table, .task/ worktree artifacts, ps aux) with no schema/version contract
clusters.architecture_notes: dashboard/ is a FastAPI app (app.py, 1.35k lines, ~40 route handlers) that is almost pure routing/proxy boilerplate; the real logic lives in dashboard/src/dashboard/data/*.py (~10.6k lines across 20 modules). Two read paths exist for orchestrator state: (1) a proper published-API path — get_merge_queue MCP tool fanned out per orchestrator in merge_queue.py:_probe_live_one/fetch_live_merge_queues (task-1606), which IS a good seam; and (2) a scraping path that is the actual hotspot — direct SQLite reads against orchestrator's data/orchestrator/runs.db events table (merge_queue.py, costs.py, metrics.py, burndown.py all open this DB and hand-write SQL against its `events`/`invocations`/`account_events` tables), plus filesystem scraping of orchestrator's .task/ worktree artifacts and `ps aux` process-list parsing (orchestrator.py). Task metadata itself, by contrast, goes through fused-memory's get_tasks MCP tool (tasks.py:fetch_tasks) — a real API, not scraped — so the coupling problem is concentrated specifically in reading orchestrator-internal state (events.db + on-disk worktree artifacts + process list), not task/memory state. The events table's `data` JSON column and `event_type`/`outcome` strings are documented only in code comments (orchestrator/src/orchestrator/event_store.py's EventType StrEnum + per-event payload-shape comments) and are never imported or referenced by the dashboard package — dashboard re-derives the same string literals independently. A second recurring defect class is time-window "now" resolution inside asyncio.gather fan-outs across multiple per-project SQLite connections: one incident (task 692) proved that letting each per-DB coroutine call datetime.now(UTC) independently causes divergent bucket boundaries and silent data loss when results are zipped; the fix (thread one `effective_now` from the aggregator entrypoint) was applied thoroughly within merge_queue.py but not propagated to sibling aggregate_* functions in burndown.py/costs.py that have the identical shape. A third pattern is duplicated infrastructure: the MCP fan-out-with-failover loop (`for url in config.fused_memory_urls: try mcp_tool_call except (…) : invalidate_session; continue`) and a TTL-cache-with-clear-hook are each hand-rolled independently in 4-5 different modules (tasks.py's own docstring explicitly calls this out as "the third copy of the pattern" and defers fixing it as out-of-scope).
clusters.cross_system_notes: Orchestrator (orchestrator/src/orchestrator/merge_queue.py, event_store.py, config.py, artifacts.py) drives dashboard fixes repeatedly: every time orchestrator adds a new free-form merge outcome string (train_partial_flip added 6wk ago in 88473b9e73, main_health_red added 4wk ago in 8fba07f70d, cas_retry added 2d ago in c1869a71a5) or changes its runs.db event shape, the dashboard's hand-maintained outcome/event-type literals in merge_queue.py silently go stale — there is no PR-linkage or shared-symbol dependency forcing a dashboard update, so drift is discovered only when someone notices bad dashboard output. Conversely the one clock-skew race dashboard did get right (task 692, fixing aggregate_queue_depth_timeseries) never fed back into a documented invariant that orchestrator or the dashboard's other aggregate_* authors could reuse, so the same shape of bug (independent datetime.now(UTC) calls inside a per-project asyncio.gather fan-out) is still latent in burndown.py and costs.py today.

findings.title: Merge-outcome vocabulary silently drifted from orchestrator's actual (unenumerated) outcome strings
findings.problem: merge_queue.py hardcodes two overlapping outcome allowlists — _CANONICAL_OUTCOMES (4 values) and _TERMINAL_MERGE_OUTCOMES (8 values, frozen at merge_queue.py:53-57) — used by outcome_distribution and, critically, by active_queued_merges (line 783: `if et == 'merge_attempt' and outcome in _TERMINAL_MERGE_OUTCOMES: continue`) to decide whether a task is still 'in_flight'. But orchestrator's _emit_merge_attempt is called with at least 18 distinct free-form strings across orchestrator/src/orchestrator/merge_queue.py ('main_health_red', 'merge_failed', 'verify_failed', 'advance_failed', 'train_incomplete', 'train_rebase_conflict', 'train_partial_flip', 'cas_failed', 'cas_retry', 'gate_retry', plus the 8 already covered) — there is no shared enum; MergeOutcome.status in merge_types.py:732 is a Literal with yet a THIRD, different set of values ('wip_halted', 'done_wip_recovery', 'unmerged_state', 'superseded', 'error' — none of which appear in either dashboard set or in the _emit_merge_attempt string set, since outcome and MergeOutcome.status are different fields entirely).
findings.proposal: Promote the merge-attempt outcome to a real closed type owned by orchestrator (e.g. an `OutcomeKind` StrEnum in merge_types.py with an explicit `is_terminal` classmethod/property), have _emit_merge_attempt accept only that enum, and have dashboard import the enum (or a small shared `orchestrator.merge_types` re-export) instead of hand-maintaining two divergent string lists. If a hard import dependency is undesirable, invert the default: classify outcomes as terminal-unless-listed (an explicit ACTIVE_ONLY allowlist for retry states like cas_retry/gate_retry) since new terminal outcomes are added far more often than new active ones, so drift fails safe instead of failing stale.
findings.bug_history_link: _TERMINAL_MERGE_OUTCOMES was defined once in 8553b388ad (~2 months ago) and never touched again per `git log -S`, while orchestrator kept adding outcome strings after that point (88473b9e73 6wk ago, 8fba07f70d 4wk ago, c1869a71a5 2d ago) — confirmed by git -S searches on both files.

findings.title: Per-DB clock-skew race fixed once (task 692) but left latent in sibling aggregators
findings.problem: merge_queue.py's aggregate/timeseries functions all accept an explicit `now` parameter and resolve `effective_now` once, threaded through every per-DB call in asyncio.gather (fixed by commit 0020b1d0ac / task 692, which explicitly documents 'eliminating the race where skewed datetime.now(UTC) calls could produce divergent label sets and silent data loss'). burndown.py's get_burndown_series (line 509) and costs.py's get_cost_trend/_cutoff (lines 33, 440) still call datetime.now(UTC) directly inside functions that ARE invoked concurrently per-project via asyncio.gather in aggregate_burndown_series and aggregate_cost_trend — the identical shape of race, unfixed.
findings.proposal: Extract the merge_queue.py pattern into a shared helper (e.g. dashboard.data.utils.resolve_now / a tiny `WindowClock` passed into every aggregate_* function) and thread a single request-scoped `now` from each app.py route handler down through burndown.py's and costs.py's aggregate_* functions exactly as merge_queue.py already does; add a repo-local grep-based CI check forbidding bare `datetime.now(UTC)` inside any function reachable from an asyncio.gather fan-out in dashboard/data/, so the next new aggregator can't reintroduce task-692's race.
findings.bug_history_link: task 692 (dashboard fix 0020b1d0ac, 'add now param to aggregate_queue_depth_timeseries, fix race') proves this exact bug class occurred and was fixed in merge_queue.py; burndown.py/costs.py were never updated to match, confirmed by grep showing raw datetime.now(UTC) still present at burndown.py:509 and costs.py:33/440 today.

findings.title: MCP fan-out-with-failover and TTL caching each reimplemented independently in 4-5 modules
findings.problem: Two policies are copy-pasted rather than centralized: (1) the 'iterate config.fused_memory_urls, try mcp_tool_call, on failure invalidate_session and continue to next URL' failover loop appears independently at 9+ call sites with inconsistent exception tuples (memory.py/tasks.py catch httpx.ConnectError/TimeoutException/HTTPStatusError/ValueError; metrics.py catches only httpx.HTTPError/ValueError); (2) the '{TTL constant, dict[str, tuple[float, T]] cache, _clear() test hook, store-only-on-success}' TTL-cache pattern is hand-rolled 3 times (tasks.py, merge_queue.py, app.py) — tasks.py's own docstring names this explicitly as tech debt deferred out of scope. A prior fix (d66f6fef79, 'harden load_task_titles cache — path normalization') added os.path.realpath keying to ONE of the three caches; the current merge_queue.py load_task_titles code no longer contains that normalization (superseded by the MCP-based fetch_tasks path), and tasks.py's own _fetch_tasks_cache keys on raw `str(project_root)` with no realpath normalization at all.
findings.proposal: Add a single `dashboard.data.mcp_client.FusedMemoryClient` (extending memory.py) that owns URL fan-out (one canonical exception tuple + invalidate_session policy) and a generic TTL-cache-with-realpath-normalized-keys; delete the 3 ad hoc caches (tasks.py._fetch_tasks_cache, merge_queue.py._task_titles_cache, app.py._task_cards_cache) and the 9 duplicated fan-out loops in favor of calling through it — this finishes the refactor tasks.py's own docstring explicitly deferred.
findings.bug_history_link: d66f6fef79 ('harden load_task_titles cache — path normalization, mutation safety, and edge-case tests') is direct evidence this exact defect class occurred once and was patched locally rather than in a shared cache abstraction.

findings.title: Dashboard re-derives orchestrator's process-launch and file-artifact formats instead of importing or being served them
files: orchestrator/src/orchestrator/config.py:93-100 (_expand_env_vars, the source of truth being duplicated)
orchestrator/src/orchestrator/artifacts.py:366-410 (read_plan/get_completed_steps, which also walks a 'prerequisites' collection read_task_artifacts ignores)

chains.name: Merge-landed vs task-done atomicity gap (the ghost-loop web)
chains.description: The merge queue advances refs/heads/main in-process; the task's status=done is written afterwards to fused-memory over MCP, and a crash between the two loses the write. Because no durable record says 'branch X landed as SHA Y for task Z', SIX+ independent detectors re-derive it forensically: workflow.py pre-PLAN (line 1642) and post-PLAN ghost-loop guards with deliberately divergent semantics and keep-in-sync comments, the 90-line _has_prior_implementation dual-signal heuristic; merge_queue.py's is_ancestor already-merged detection inside classify_and_merge (verified ~line 1043-1077); scheduler.py's four-class rejection exception family (verified: SetTaskStatusRejected/TerminalExitRejection/DoneGateRejection/ProvenanceValidationRejection at scheduler.py:93-160) mirroring fused-memory's server-side phantom-done/terminal-exit/provenance gates; and harness's find_merge_marker commit-subject grep inside _reconcile_one_stranded. Fix history: 7dfe0e69bc, e6d958a133, 492bb8f126, dc33b760c8, tasks 846/851/882/883/954/1141 — every one a patch on the same missing guarantee. MERGES: merge-queue finding 3, workflow finding 1, the merge-marker-archaeology half of harness finding 5, and the find_merge_marker clause of scheduler finding 2 all describe this one root cause from four sides.
chains.proposal: One write-ahead landed journal: extend MergeQueueStore (it already durably journals accepted requests) with a landed table (task_id, branch_tip_sha, advanced_sha, ts) written and fsynced BEFORE the CAS ref update in the same critical section (adopting the workflow reviewer's ordering with the merge-queue reviewer's substrate). Consumers: (1) a startup reconciler drives status=done with merged-provenance from unconsumed rows, closing the lost-callback window; (2) scheduler/workflow's three already-merged guards collapse to one MergeProvenance.lookup(task_id) + one is_ancestor confirmation; (3) harness's find_merge_marker archaeology dies; (4) fused-memory's server-side gates stay as boundary defense-in-depth. Guard count drops from ~6 heuristics to 1 lookup.

chains.name: No task-status transition authority — dead-end states recovered by heuristic sweeps two subsystems away
chains.description: tasks.status is free TEXT with no legality table anywhere; the vocabulary is hand-duplicated in 4 modules (orchestrator/task_status.py with a 'DRIFT RISK' comment, fm task_interceptor.py:115, reconciliation/task_filter.py, plus workflow's WorkflowState/WorkflowOutcome parallel vocabularies), and 'who may write which transition' exists only as spot server gates. Consequence chain, verified in code: escalation server's resolve_issue(action='resume') contract is 'stays in-progress' (server.py:521) while the scheduler dispatches only 'pending' — so memberless resumes strand tasks forever (esc-2073-15); harness then compensates with seven reconciliation sweeps inferring claimant liveness from plan.lock/pid; and task 1883 overloaded 'in-progress' with a second meaning via metadata.infra_hold, enforced by two hand-matched flag checks (harness.py:3446 and 8464) that a third caller can silently miss. MERGES: scheduler finding 2, workflow finding 3, fm-task-layer finding 5, escalation findings 1 and 4, and the sweep-proliferation half of harness finding 5 — one missing authority producing compensations in five subsystems.
chains.proposal: One transition authority at the existing single write chokepoint: shared/src/shared/task_statuses.py exports a StrEnum + a (from_status, to_status, actor_class) legality table; fused-memory's TaskInterceptor (which already gates terminal-exit) enforces it and returns typed rejections instead of silent no-ops; add a first-class claimant field (run_id + heartbeat) stamped at dispatch so 'stranded' becomes a queryable predicate, shrinking the harness sweeps to 'heartbeat expired → pending'. Escalation's resolve actions and the infra_hold exemption become table rows (an explicit in-progress-hold-infra sub-state) instead of scattered flag checks; workflow's client-side machine becomes a thin validator over the same shared table.

chains.name: Task metadata is an unversioned cross-process schema — drift ships silently in both directions
chains.description: metadata is a schemaless JSON blob carrying ~15 load-bearing keys across the process boundary, parsed by 8+ divergent best-effort parsers. Verified live instance: orchestrator's DeterministicRunner writes done_provenance.kind='deterministic-deploy-scheduled' (deterministic_runner.py:994) which fused-memory's _VALID_PROVENANCE_KINDS (task_interceptor.py:3548) had to be patched to accept after every own-unit deploy silently blocked (9493fa073d, tasks 1976/1982); before_done.cwd was never validated so detached self-restarts exited 127 (task 2105); memory_hints needed a shipped-drift repair shim. The same gap produces workflow's eight untyped anti-thrash counters with best-effort persistence, and the DeterministicRunner's four-stamp implicit deploy state machine that harness must reverse-engineer via _is_stranded_deterministic_shape and that the scheduler reviewer showed aliases ANY task-scoped escalation as 'human resolved the deploy'. MERGES: fm-task-layer findings 1 and 7, harness finding 2, scheduler finding 1, and workflow finding 5 — all are shapes of 'no shared, versioned metadata contract'.
chains.proposal: shared/src/shared/task_metadata.py: a versioned pydantic TaskMetadata with typed sub-models (BeforeDone, DoneProvenance, DeployState with an explicit phase enum + persisted verify baseline, RetryLedger, ExternalDep, MemoryHints) and ONE parse function with one failure policy. Enforce at the single write boundary (SqliteTaskBackend add/update validate the blob; kind-fields also guarded on update_task per fm-task-layer finding 7); orchestrator imports the same model for reads. DeterministicRunner writes phase+evidence atomically as one key and scopes escalation queries by its sentinel agent_role, killing the ever_escalated aliasing; harness sweeps branch on the explicit phase instead of stamp archaeology.

chains.name: Escalation queue as untyped cross-process RPC — action semantics reconstructed by each consumer
chains.description: The escalation server validates only the action string (RESOLVE_ACTIONS, server.py:130) and flips record status; WHAT each action does to a task lives entirely in harness.py's independently-evolving interpretation (_ACTION_TARGETS at harness.py:8069, _cascade_unblock_member at 8428) with silently-failing preconditions — the exact mechanism of esc-2073-15 and the regression of the 2026-06 repend-state-machine PRD once task 1883 added branches outside it. The same missing typed channel forces workflow's steward-outcome forensics (five probes over queue side effects + timestamp windows, workflow.py:7913-7998) and DeterministicRunner's ever_escalated = get_by_task(task_id) with no role filter, so a starvation-watchdog escalation aliases as deploy-resolution proof. The level gate is caller-declared (X-Escalation-Levels header sent only by the orchestrator's own watcher) and promote_to_l2's create side has no check at all. MERGES: escalation findings 1/2/3, workflow finding 2, scheduler finding 1's escalation-scoping half, and harness's _WATCHER_ESCALATION_HEADERS lockstep note.
chains.proposal: Three moves. (1) One authoritative transition table (escalation exports it; consumers import) so resolve_issue rejects illegal action/state combos loudly and harness computes effects from the same table — precondition failures become typed rejections, never DEBUG logs. (2) Typed result channels replace queue forensics: StewardOutcome sum type returned to the owning workflow; add an agent_role filter to EscalationQueue.get_by_task and scope all DeterministicRunner queries by its 'orchestrator-deterministic' sentinel. (3) Server-side role→allowed-levels mapping gating BOTH resolve_issue and promote_to_l2 — with header-less/interactive callers explicitly mapped to full human capability (see contradictions).

chains.name: Claude CLI's unstructured contract — cap/wedge classification scattered across five sites and two hand-rolled retry loops
chains.description: The upstream CLI exposes no machine-readable rate-limit/liveness/tool-policy signal, so classification is prose-scraping duplicated with divergent rules in 5 places (UsageGate.detect_cap_hit, _run_probe's deliberate prefix-only asymmetry, invoke_with_cap_retry's heuristic + NON_CAP markers, _parse_claude_output, classify_agent_failure); the steward hand-rolls a second cap-retry loop already divergent on every policy axis (no wedge guard, no auth routing, fixed cooldown); AllAccountsCappedException escapes to four independent catch sites (verified: workflow.py:1919, steward.py:653, review_checkpoint.py:192, dry_run_unblock.py:341); the stale-session wedge invariant is enforced independently in shared/cli_invoke.py AND fused-memory's reconciliation agent_loop.py:368; and workflow's run() ends in a seven-clause exception ladder re-classifying failures other subsystems raised. The 10x cap-message whack-a-mole and 4x probe-slot-leak themes are both downstream of this one missing seam. MERGES: shared-infra findings 1/2/3/5, workflow finding 4, and the fm-recon agent_loop duplicate.
chains.proposal: One shared classification seam: shared/invocation_outcome.py with an InvocationOutcome sum type and a single classifier holding ALL string tables (probe policy = strict_confirm flag, not a second loop), structured fields (is_error, api_error_status==429) taking precedence over prose with a loud 'cap_prose_only'/'resets_parse_failed' event when only the fallback fires. InvokeSlot.report(outcome) performs the matching gate transition AND settles the slot atomically (kills the private reach-ins and slot-leak class); the account-phase enum + single _transition() function replaces the 6-flag bag. Delete the steward loop into invoke_with_cap_retry (add rebuild_prompt + max_cap_retries hooks). Downstream, workflow's exception ladder collapses to one classify_failure→BlockDisposition table consumed by _mark_blocked, steward, review_checkpoint, and dry_run_unblock.

chains.name: Missing write-time guarantees in the memory stores — recon and memory_service both patch with post-hoc sweeps and an LLM nonce arms race
chains.description: Two instances of one pattern: the store lacks a write-time guarantee, so consumers stack reactive compensation. (a) MemoryService silently dedups ~0.92-cosine-similar writes with no system-write exemption, so recon keeps its control plane (6 marker/summary record kinds) in Mem0 and teaches the LLM CSPRNG summary_nonce/retry_nonce construction via prompt prose (verified: prompts/stage2.py:237-296 narrates the dedup threshold and the 'write 74b902f8' loss), then Python verify→repair→reconstructs swallowed writes and runs FOUR separate marker GC sweeps; the flag_dedup module docstring narrates seven stacked compensations. (b) graphiti_core has no exact-name entity resolution and merge_entities copies edge uuids, so memory_service chains four best-effort dedup sweeps after every add_episode (verified: _dedup_episode_edges/_dedup_episode_nodes at memory_service.py:484/531) and every edge query hand-rolls WITH DISTINCT — already gotten wrong twice (cfed95c706, task 2084). The duplicates recon can't fix get filed as tasks into the orchestrator's TDD pipeline, which must refuse them (operational-dedup /unblock class, task 2085). MERGES: fm-recon findings 1/2, fm-memory findings 1/2, and the fm-recon↔fm-memory dedup cross-notes.
chains.proposal: Fix the guarantee, delete the compensations: (1) add_memory(dedup_exempt=True) enforced server-side for recon-stage agent_ids, then delete all nonce prompt machinery and the verify/repair/reconstruct chain — Python writes cycle summaries deterministically post-stage; (2) move recon's marker/suppression/summary ledger to a SQLite ReconLedgerStore (transactional UPSERT replaces write/confirm/delete; four GC sweeps become one DELETE), keeping Mem0 as a narrative mirror only; (3) in graphiti_client, resolve-or-create entities via exact-name lookup before minting (uniqueness constraint or per-group lock) and mint fresh uuids on edge redirect with superseded_edge_uuid audit — restoring uuid-unique edges kills the hand-rolled DISTINCT class.

chains.name: Git-substrate invariants enforced by convention: unguarded prune, divergent lane teardown, and .task/ in-tree
chains.description: Three limbs of one root: git-level safety invariants live in comments, not chokepoints. (a) The task-2099 registration-wipe guard lives ONLY inside prune_worktrees; six raw `git worktree prune` sites bypass it (verified: git_ops.py:3824, 4341, 4426, 5365, reap_interactive_worktrees, harness substrate-gate) — the merge-lane sites run during exactly the mount-down window 2099 guards, recreating the CRITICAL Jul-3/4 incident through a side door; verify.py's probe worktrees state 'INTENTIONALLY NO prune (DD5)' three times as comments enforced nowhere. (b) acquire_warm_lane's top-level except still does bare pool.release with no HEAD detach, re-creating the task-2062 'already used by worktree at _lane-K' collision class the named paths were fixed for. (c) .task/ sidecars live inside agent-writable worktrees, defended by six redundant guards across git_ops/merge_gates/artifacts/workflow that still leak (reify esc-4920-163). Related upstream gap: fused-memory re-mints deleted task ids, which is the sole reason worktree_identity.py and the identity-adoption guards exist. MERGES: git-worktrees findings 1/2/4, verify finding 6, and the git-worktrees cross-note on task-id recycling.
chains.proposal: Chokepoints plus one relocation: (1) GitOps._prune_registrations(context) as the ONLY site containing the prune argv, gated on pool health, enforced by a grep-guard test asserting exactly one occurrence (repo already uses this idiom); ephemeral probe worktrees get a shared context manager with a PROTECTED_PREFIXES registry consulted by all reapers. (2) One _abort_lane_acquisition teardown primitive (commit-or-discard, detach, branch-retention, release) routed through by every fault exit including the catch-all. (3) Move .task/ out-of-tree to <worktree_base>/.task-meta/<name>/ (quarantine_base precedent), making contamination structurally impossible and deleting the six-guard stack. (4) Upstream: make fused-memory task ids monotonic/never-recycled, then delete worktree_identity.py's title heuristic.

chains.name: Merge-queue permits and lifecycle tracked by census instead of ownership — false-positive detector storms
chains.description: Included as a chain because its blast radius crosses into operations: anonymous semaphore permits + lifecycle-by-container-membership force a five-location census audit (_inflight_speculative_count) where every new await point creates an invisible window and a new false-positive class — tasks 2063/2068/2096 each added another side-field (_redispatch, _finalizing_head, _dispatching_item), and the I4 esc-__merge_resource_leak__ alarms that consumed human triage (operator memory 2026-07-05) were detector FPs from exactly this gap. Callers must thread release_resources/chain_failed flags ('release_resources=not _entry_released') to avoid double-release, and snapshot() has already diverged from the audit once (task 2068). MERGES: merge-queue findings 1 and 2 (same root: no owned state), with finding 4 (fake extraction seams frozen by test monkeypatch paths) as the reason the 17-task refactor couldn't fix it.
chains.proposal: SpecPermit token owned by a PermitLedger (idempotent release(token), conservation structural by construction — census and side-fields die) stored ON the item through every queue; an ItemLifecycle registry with a legal-transition table replacing the four side-fields and three parallel status mechanisms, so snapshot/audit/liveness are single reads that cannot disagree. Precondition: finish the satellite extraction along state lines (owning objects per satellite, repoint the 7 monkeypatch string paths once, import-linter contract banning reach-back imports) so the ledger has a real home.

chains.name: Dashboard scrapes orchestrator internals with no shared vocabulary — silent staleness by design
chains.description: Orchestrator emits ~18 free-form merge-outcome strings (three added AFTER dashboard's _TERMINAL_MERGE_OUTCOMES froze: 88473b9e73, 8fba07f70d, c1869a71a5 two days ago) and dashboard's in_flight logic silently mis-classifies the new ones; dashboard also re-implements orchestrator's ${VAR} config expansion regex, ps-aux process discovery, and .task/ plan parsing (missing the prerequisites collection orchestrator's own artifacts.py walks). Same class as the fm-task-layer overrides-store dual-implementation (17 'Mirrors orchestrator/...:<line>' comments) and the status-vocabulary quadruplication: cross-package contracts maintained by hand-copy because no shared home was used, despite shared/ already being consumed by both sides (shared.usage_gate, shared.locking precedent cited by dashboard's own scheduler.py). MERGES: dashboard findings 1/4, fm-task-layer finding 3, and the status-vocab limb of chain 2.
chains.proposal: Adopt shared/ as the single sanctioned cross-package home: OutcomeKind StrEnum with is_terminal (orchestrator emits only the enum; dashboard imports it — or, minimum viable, invert to terminal-unless-listed so drift fails safe), move _expand_env_vars and the overrides/park-eviction store logic into shared/ with sync+async adapters, and replace ps-aux/.task scraping with a small orchestrator status MCP tool mirroring the proven get_merge_queue seam (task 1606). Also thread the task-692 effective_now pattern into burndown.py/costs.py where the identical gather clock-skew race is still latent (verified by the reviewer at burndown.py:509, costs.py:33/440).

top_priorities: 1. Write-ahead landed journal in MergeQueueStore (task_id → landed SHA, fsynced before the CAS main advance) + startup reconciler — one medium-effort change that collapses ~6 ghost-loop/phantom-done/false-done detectors across merge-queue, workflow, scheduler, and harness, the single largest cross-system compensation web (20+ historical fix tasks).

2. Cheap chokepoint bundle in git_ops (days, not weeks): single guarded _prune_registrations site enforced by a grep-guard test, one _abort_lane_acquisition teardown primitive covering the catch-all path, and a PROTECTED_PREFIXES registry for ephemeral worktrees — directly prevents recurrence of two already-lived CRITICAL incident classes (registration wipe, stale-checkout collision) at near-zero risk.

3. Server-side task-status transition authority: shared StrEnum + (from,to,actor) legality table enforced in fused-memory's TaskInterceptor with typed rejections, plus a first-class claimant/heartbeat field — kills the stranded-task class (resume-leaves-in-progress, infra_hold overload, vocabulary drift) and shrinks harness's seven sweeps to one heartbeat check.

4. Versioned shared TaskMetadata schema (shared/task_metadata.py, typed BeforeDone/DoneProvenance/DeployState/RetryLedger sub-models, validated at the backend write boundary) — kills the bidirectional schema-drift class (provenance-kind rejections, before_done.cwd 127s, memory_hints repair shims, stamp-archaeology deploy recovery) that currently ships silently.

5. One InvocationOutcome classifier + atomic InvokeSlot.report + AccountPhase transition function in shared/, then delete the steward's duplicate cap-retry loop and collapse workflow's seven-clause exception ladder into a classify_failure→BlockDisposition table — ends the cap-string whack-a-mole (10x), probe-slot leaks (4x), and AllAccountsCapped escape (4x) themes in one seam.

6. Recon control-plane off Mem0: dedup-exempt server-enforced system-write path + SQLite ReconLedgerStore — deletes the nonce arms race, the verify/repair/reconstruct chain, and four marker GC sweeps in the repo's hottest fix surface (871 reconciliation commits since April), with the graphiti write-time exact-name resolution as the companion fix on the store side.

7. Merge-queue SpecPermit ledger + ItemLifecycle transition registry (after the one-time monkeypatch-path migration unfreezes the seams) — makes permit conservation and lifecycle state structural, ending the invisible-window false-positive class that has been generating both fix tasks (2063/2068/2096) and human triage load (I4 alarm storms).

8. 'Parse, don't validate' typed-value sweep, each item small and independently landable: ProjectScope (kills the 10x project_id/project_root swap class at compile time via existing pyright gates), QueuedBranch (kills branch shape-tolerance retrofits), FailureCategory enum + policy table (kills the 5-registry category sync dance), AccountLease (kills cost misattribution).
cross_system.contradictions: Four substantive conflicts, all resolvable. (1) THREE HOMES FOR THE TRANSITION TABLE: the workflow reviewer proposes a client-side WorkflowStateMachine, the scheduler reviewer puts the (from,to,actor) table in fused-memory's TaskInterceptor, and the escalation reviewer proposes escalation/state_machine.py as the authority. Resolution: the enforcement floor must live at the single durable write chokepoint (TaskInterceptor) with the table itself defined in shared/ so escalation's resolve_issue and workflow's local machine consume the SAME table as thin validators — three tables would recreate the drift they're meant to fix. (2) MERGE-PROVENANCE SUBSTRATE: merge-queue reviewer says MergeQueueStore landed-outbox 'in the same code path as' the CAS advance; workflow reviewer says event_store/git-note journal 'ordered BEFORE the ref update, fsynced'. Same fix — resolve to MergeQueueStore (already durable, already journals the accept side) with the workflow reviewer's stricter write-ahead ordering, since write-after re-opens the crash window the whole chain exists to close. (3) ESCALATION LEVEL GATE VS THE HEADER-LESS-HUMAN CONVENTION: the proposal to derive allowed levels from server-side caller identity (default-deny on unknown callers) conflicts with the deployed, deliberate design where header-LESS sessions are the human channel — operator memory documents that only header-less sessions may close L2s and the autonomous watcher is capped at {0,1}. A naive default-deny would lock humans out of L2 closure (repeating the 'can't close esc-2087-2' pain). Resolution: role-mapped ceilings for identified automation callers, header-less explicitly mapped to full human capability, and gate promote_to_l2's create side the same way. (4) DUPLICATION DOCTRINE VS SHARED/: task_interceptor.py:115's stated policy 'duplication is cheaper than cross-package coupling' contradicts five reviewers' proposals (status enum, TaskMetadata, overrides store, invocation outcome, dashboard OutcomeKind) AND is already violated by the CI drift-guard test that imports cross-package. Resolution: retire the doctrine; shared/ is the proven sanctioned home (shared.usage_gate, shared.locking precedents). Minor notes: harness and scheduler reviewers independently proposed the identical SchedulerCallbacks constructor-dataclass seam (agreement, merge into one task, and fold workflow finding 8's three-facade protocol split into the same seam work); the dashboard reviewer's primary proposal (hard dashboard→orchestrator import) conflicts with their own fallback and with (4) — use shared/ or the fail-safe terminal-unless-listed inversion. Data note: the mined-themes list contains one obvious test fixture ('test theme'/'test evidence', escalation, count 2) — disregarded.
